titleStmt.title: Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the White House

div.head: 474. Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the White House
div.p: 2. Memorandum for the President from George P. Shultz.

3. Visit to Venezuela, February 1–2, 1984. The inaugural ceremonies here were the center piece of the day, well attended and promising. President Lusinchi’s inaugural address was moderate and statesmanlike. I had an excellent private meeting with the Central American core four Foreign Ministers and bilaterals with the Presidents of Argentina and Bolivia.

4. A dozen heads of government and more than 70 delegations, including numerous representatives of the Soviet bloc, marked Venezuela’s global reach.
Behind the fanfare, however, this is a country aware that it is in deep economic trouble but which remains committed to Western values and hemispheric stability.

5. Lusinchi’s inaugural address was statesmanlike and confident. In domestic matters, he stressed the need to put Venezuela’s finances in order, making an appeal for the support of all parties for the “years of penitence” that lie ahead because of Venezuela’s debt. He made no cheap shots at the banks.

6. On foreign affairs, Lusinchi was equally moderate. On Central America, he named no names, but made clear that Venezuela would continue to support democracy. Indeed, in what could be construed as an indirect warning to the Nicaraguans, he stressed that support for democracy elsewhere is a principle enshrined in the preamble to Venezuela’s Constitution.
7. I will be seeing Lusinchi for breakfast February 3.

8. The highlight of my private meetings was breakfast with the Foreign Ministers of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, and Guatemala. Though we had word of some personal and tactical tensions among them, we readily reached agreement on the need for close coordination to keep pressure on Nicaragua in the Contadora process. And although the civilians are generally not up on the military side, they seemed aware of the special importance of cooperation against the Salvadoran guerrillas before the elections. The two areas we need to work on are first, once again, to get the resources to do the job, both economically and militarily, and [garble] convince the
Guatemalans that we are serious and that they will only hurt themselves if they stay aloof from the common cause.

9. Nicaragua’s Ortega was in town telling everyone who would listen that we were the source of all evil and that Kissinger had secretly recommended an invasion of both El Salvador and Nicaragua. That line is wearing a bit thin even down here. I took advantage of my press conference to point out that Ortega’s imagination was playing tricks on him, but that he had every reason to be worried after the way the Sandinistas had betrayed Nicaragua.

10. My bilaterals with the Presidents of Bolivia and Argentina were less productive. Bolivia’s Siles stressed his country’s economic problems, which are [garble] and not all his fault, and said he would do better in the future. I said we understood and supported his role in returning Bolivia to democracy, but were concerned by the drug trafficking and the growing influence of the left. We will see.

11. Argentina’s Alfonsin was one of the media heroes here and obviously a man to watch. But my meeting with him was cut short by Caracas traffic and ceremonies. The Falklands issue remains high on the Argentina agenda, as does the debt issue, and Alfonsin seems to be looking for political hay on both. Alfonsin insisted that a NATO military base on the Falklands would lead to a Soviet response. I assured him that we are not considering turning the Falklands into a NATO base. Time ran out before we could get further. Alfonsin remembered very warmly the Vice President’s visit for his inauguration.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, Executive Secretariat, NSC Country File, Latin America/Central, Venezuela (02/03/1984–12/17/1984). Secret; Immediate; Nodis. Sent from aboard the Delegation’s aircraft. Printed from a copy that indicates the original was received in the White House Situation Room. Reagan wrote his initials at the top of the first page. Shultz visited Caracas, February 1–3, to attend the inauguration of Lusinchi and meet with Central American Foreign Ministers. In telegram 475 from Caracas, January 17, the Embassy reported on Walters’ January 16 meeting with Lusinchi, who “devoted much of a warm and friendly meeting to a discussion of his many contacts with the Venezuelan military since the elections and to his satisfaction that the military was solidly behind Venezuela’s democratic processes and his presidency.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, N840001–0420)
See Department of State Bulletin, April 1984, pp. 20–22.
